p:AUT: Austria uses the euro: the European Central Bank sets its interest rates, for the 21 euro countries together, with the Oesterreichische Nationalbank taking part; the ECB is one of 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. The national bank owns its banknote printer, OeBS, which cooperates with two other central-bank-owned printers. Managers of OeBS paid kickbacks to win orders, overcharging Azerbaijan's central bank by 20 percent and Syria's by 14 percent, about 14 million euros. Seven were convicted in October 2014; after a retrial, a Vienna court in February 2018 gave Wolf and Miller 18-month suspended sentences and Meyer 21 months suspended, and acquitted former deputy governor Duchatczek. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, ruled that ECB president Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a club of central bankers and private bankers, was maladministration; the ECB declined to drop it. In 2015 a speech by board member Coeure on front-loading asset purchases reached a private London audience the evening before publication; the ECB called this an internal procedure error. BDO Assurance, elected on 23 March 2023, audited the bank's 2025 accounts. The government that took office in 2017, the People's Party with the Freedom Party, planned to take banking supervision away from the bank. In April 2019 the bank said publicly that this threatened its financial independence: the draft law would have paid 95 percent of its profits to the federal government instead of the 90 percent then in force, which it said cuts its ability to build reserves, and it expected supervision costs to rise under more complicated structures that included three new sections inside the Finance Ministry. The Finance Ministry answered that it was following European best practice, that a payout rate of 95 percent or more existed in countries including the Netherlands, and that the change was structural and aimed at efficiency rather than personal. The reform did not take effect and the bank still supervises banks. Austria scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:NOR: Norges Bank issues the Norwegian krone and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital has been held by central banks alone since private shares were bought back in 2001. Both recorded cases come out of one hiring. On 24 March 2020 the Executive Board appointed Nicolai Tangen, who had started the hedge fund AKO Capital in 2005, to run Norges Bank Investment Management, which manages the country's oil fund. The bank's Supervisory Council warned that the hire risked breaking laws, rules and guidelines, saying Tangen still appeared to be AKO Capital's main owner with voting control, although the bank said he had cut those ties. After the Storting's finance committee raised the same concern, the Executive Board revised his terms in August 2020: he would give up his holding in AKO Capital LLP and hand it and its dividend rights to the charitable AKO Foundation, and hold his personal fund assets as bank deposits. Supervisory Board chair Julie Brodtkorb said guidelines, regulations and laws had been breached; Executive Board chair Oystein Olsen said the board had thought the existing contract was enough but accepted that the Storting took a different view. Tangen could take office on 1 September. Ernst & Young audits the bank from the 2022 financial year for six years, and at the end of 2025 103 organisations ran outside mandates worth 1,062 billion kroner. Notes were printed by Oberthur Fiduciaire in France from 2016 to 2019 and, from 2020, by Crane NXT in Malta. A commission appointed by the Ministry of Finance and chaired by Svein Gjedrem, a former governor of the bank, proposed in late June 2017 that the oil fund be managed by a separate statutory entity outside Norges Bank, which would have taken away the largest thing the bank does. Its reasoning was that central banking and investment management differ in nature, that both had grown and now placed greater demands on the board, senior management and the organisation, and that separate bodies could tailor their skills to each task. The bank's own leadership and the fund's split in public: governor Oystein Olsen wanted the fund kept inside Norges Bank, while the fund's chief executive Yngve Slyngstad was reported as believing it should be taken out. The Ministry of Finance rejected the proposal and decided the management should stay in the central bank, on the reasoning that Norges Bank enjoyed a high level of trust in Norway and internationally and that its performance in both roles had been good over time; the Central Bank Act the Storting passed on 28 May 2019, in force from 1 January 2020, left the bank both responsibilities. Norway scores 20 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
